p.src: Now the king of the Western Qiang, Che Liji, had sent tribute every year since Cao Cao’s time. Under him were two chief officers, one civil and one military: the civil officer was Chancellor Yadan, and the military officer was Marshal Yueji. When the Wei envoy arrived in the kingdom bearing gold, pearls, and a letter, he first went to see Chancellor Yadan. He presented the gifts and fully explained that Wei had come to ask for aid. Yadan brought him before the king and presented the letter and gifts. After Che Liji had read the letter, he assembled his officers for deliberation. Yadan said, “We have always maintained relations with Wei. Now Commander Cao asks for our aid and promises a marriage alliance besides. It is only fitting that we consent.” Che Liji followed his advice and commanded Yadan and Marshal Yueji to raise one hundred and fifty thousand Qiang troops, all skilled in the use of bows, crossbows, spears, swords, caltrops, flying hammers, and other weapons. They also had war wagons clad and studded with iron plates, carrying provisions, weapons, and other equipment. Some were drawn by camels and others by mules or horses, and their force was called the “Iron Wagon Army.” The two took leave of the king and led their army straight toward Xiping Pass.

p.src: Han Zhen, the Shu general guarding the pass, urgently sent a messenger with a dispatch to inform Kongming. On receiving the report, Kongming asked his generals, “Who dares go and drive back the Qiang army?” Zhang Bao and Guan Xing answered, “We are willing to go.” Kongming said, “You two may wish to go, but you do not know the roads.” He then summoned Ma Dai and said, “You have long lived in that region and know the nature of the Qiang well. You can serve as their guide.” He raised fifty thousand picked troops and sent Ma Dai together with Guan Xing and Zhang Bao. Guan Xing, Zhang Bao, and the others led the army away. After several days’ march, they encountered the Qiang army. Guan Xing first led over a hundred horsemen up a hillside to observe. He saw the Qiang linking their iron wagons end to end and forming camps wherever they halted. Weapons were arrayed all over the wagons, making them resemble the walls of a city. Guan Xing studied them for a long while but could devise no way to defeat them, so he returned to camp to consult Zhang Bao and Ma Dai. Ma Dai said, “Let us wait until tomorrow, face them in battle, and observe their true strength before forming another plan.” Early the next morning, they divided the army into three columns: Guan Xing in the center, Zhang Bao on the left, and Ma Dai on the right. All three advanced together. From the Qiang formation Marshal Yueji rode forth boldly, an iron hammer in his hand and a finely carved bow hanging at his waist. Guan Xing signaled all three columns to advance straight ahead. Suddenly the Qiang troops appeared on both flanks while iron wagons poured from the center like a surging tide, and bows and crossbows discharged all at once. The Shu army suffered a crushing defeat. Ma Dai’s and Zhang Bao’s forces were the first to retreat. Guan Xing’s force was enveloped by the Qiang and driven under encirclement toward the northwest.

p.src: Caught in the heart of the encirclement, Guan Xing charged left and right but could not break free. The iron wagons enclosed him densely, like the walls of a city. The Shu soldiers could not come to one another’s aid. Guan Xing sought a path of escape among the mountain valleys. As night drew near, he saw a mass of black banners swarming toward him. A Qiang general brandishing an iron hammer shouted, “Young fool, do not flee! I am Marshal Yueji!” Guan Xing fled ahead, spurring his horse with all his might, but found his way barred by a broken ravine and had no choice but to turn and fight Yueji. But Guan Xing was shaken with fear and could not withstand him, so he fled toward the ravine. Yueji caught up and swung his iron hammer. Guan Xing dodged in haste, and the blow struck his horse on the haunch. The horse toppled into the ravine, and Guan Xing fell into the water. Suddenly there came a crash, and behind him Yueji and his horse inexplicably tumbled into the water together. Guan Xing struggled to his feet in the water and looked up to see a mighty general on the bank driving back the Qiang troops. Guan Xing raised his sword to cut down Yueji, but Yueji leapt through the water and escaped. Guan Xing took Yueji’s horse, led it onto the bank, set its saddle and bridle in order, then grasped his sword and mounted. He saw that the general was still pursuing and slaughtering the Qiang troops ahead. Guan Xing thought, “This man saved my life; I must meet him,” and urged his horse after him. As he drew near, he dimly saw amid the clouds and mist a mighty general whose face was the hue of a ripe date and whose brows resembled sleeping silkworms. He wore a green robe and golden armor, carried the Green Dragon saber, rode the Red Hare, and stroked his splendid beard. He recognized him unmistakably as his father, Lord Guan. Guan Xing was astounded. Suddenly Lord Guan pointed southeast and said, “My son, hasten along this road. I shall protect you until you return to camp.” As soon as he had spoken, he vanished. Guan Xing hurried southeast. At midnight, a body of troops suddenly arrived. It was Zhang Bao, who asked Guan Xing, “Did you see my second uncle?” Guan Xing said, “How did you know?” Zhang Bao replied, “The Iron Wagon Army was pressing me hard when suddenly I saw my uncle descend from the sky. He frightened off the Qiang troops and pointed out a road, saying, ‘Follow this road and rescue my son.’ That is why I led my troops straight here in search of you.” Guan Xing related what had happened to him as well, and together they marveled and sighed. The two returned to camp together. Ma Dai came to meet them and said, “There is no stratagem by which we can drive this army back. I shall hold the stockade while you two report to the Chancellor and ask him to devise a plan to defeat them.” Thereupon Guan Xing and Zhang Bao traveled through the night to see Kongming and gave him a full account of the affair.

p.src: Kongming at once ordered Zhao Yun and Wei Yan each to lead a force away and lie in ambush. Then he mustered thirty thousand troops, took Jiang Wei, Zhang Yi, Guan Xing, and Zhang Bao with him, and personally came to Ma Dai’s camp, where he settled in. The next day he observed from a high mound and saw an unbroken chain of iron wagons, with men and horses ranging back and forth at speed. Kongming said, “This will not be difficult to defeat.” He summoned Ma Dai and Zhang Yi and instructed them in detail what they were to do. After the two had gone, he summoned Jiang Wei and asked, “Boyue, do you know how to defeat these wagons?” Jiang Wei replied, “The Qiang rely solely upon brute courage. What could they know of subtle stratagems?” Kongming laughed and said, “You understand my mind. Dark-red clouds now cover the sky and the north wind blows fiercely. Snow is about to fall, and my plan can be put into effect.” He then ordered Guan Xing and Zhang Bao to lead troops away and take up ambush positions. He ordered Jiang Wei to lead troops out to battle, but whenever the Iron Wagon Army advanced, he was to turn and retreat. At the camp entrance, banners alone were set up as a deception, with no soldiers or horses stationed there. Thus all preparations were complete.

p.src: It was then the end of the twelfth month, and sure enough, a heavy snow fell from the heavens. Jiang Wei led his troops out, while Yueji advanced with his iron-chariot force. Jiang Wei immediately retreated. When the Qiang troops reached the stockade, Jiang Wei withdrew from its rear. The Qiang troops came right up outside the stockade to inspect it. Hearing the sound of a zither within and seeing banners standing on all four empty walls, they hurried back to report to Yueji. Yueji grew suspicious and dared not advance rashly. Prime Minister Yadan said, “This is merely one of Zhuge Liang’s tricks—a hollow display meant to make us suspect an ambush. We can attack it.” Yueji led his troops to the stockade and saw Kongming carrying his zither onto a cart, then entering the camp with a few horsemen before fleeing toward the rear. The Qiang troops rushed through the stockade gates and pursued beyond the mountain pass, where they glimpsed the small cart disappearing into the woods. Yadan told Yueji, “Even if troops like these have set an ambush, there is nothing to fear.” They therefore led the main army in pursuit. They also saw all of Jiang Wei’s troops fleeing across the snow. Yueji flew into a rage and urged his men to pursue with all speed. Snow blanketed the mountain road, making it appear level as far as the eye could see. In the midst of the pursuit, a sudden report came that Shu troops had emerged from behind the mountain. Yadan said, “Even if there is this small band in ambush, what is there to fear?” He concerned himself only with driving the troops onward. Suddenly there came a tremendous crash, as though mountains had collapsed and the earth had split, and all the Qiang troops plunged into hidden pits and trenches; the iron chariots behind were rolling at great speed and could not be stopped in time, so they piled into the men ahead, trampling one another. Just as the rear ranks hurried to turn back, Zhang Bao charged out on the right and Guan Xing on the left, while ten thousand crossbows loosed at once; from the rear, the three forces of Jiang Wei, Ma Dai, and Zhang Yi also came attacking. The iron-chariot troops fell into utter chaos. Marshal Yueji fled toward a valley behind the mountain, only to encounter Guan Xing; after a single exchange, Guan Xing raised his blade with a mighty shout and cut him down from his horse. Prime Minister Yadan had already been captured alive by Ma Dai and was brought under guard to the main camp. The Qiang troops scattered and fled. Kongming took his seat in the command tent, and Ma Dai brought Yadan before him. Kongming ordered the guards to remove his bonds, gave him wine to calm his fright, and consoled him with kindly words. Yadan was deeply moved by his kindness. Kongming said, “My lord is the Emperor of the Great Han. He has now commanded me to punish the rebels; why, then, do you assist the traitors instead? I shall now release you. Return and tell your ruler: our states are neighbors, and we should bind ourselves in lasting friendship. Do not heed the words of rebels.” He then returned to Yadan all the captured Qiang soldiers, chariots, horses, weapons, and equipment, and released them all to return home. They all bowed in gratitude and departed. Kongming led the two armies through the night toward the main camp at Mount Qi, ordering Guan Xing and Zhang Bao to lead their forces ahead; at the same time, he sent a man bearing a memorial to report the victory.

p.src: Meanwhile, Cao Zhen had been awaiting news of the Qiang for several days when scouts suddenly came to report: “The Shu troops have struck camp, packed their equipment, and set out.” Guo Huai rejoiced and said, “They are withdrawing because the Qiang troops attacked them.” They therefore divided their forces into two columns and gave chase. The Shu troops fled in disorder ahead, with the Wei troops pursuing behind. As the vanguard commander Cao Zun pressed the pursuit, drums suddenly thundered and a body of troops swept into view; the great general at their head was Wei Yan, who shouted, “Rebels, do not flee!” Cao Zun was greatly alarmed, but spurred his horse forward to engage him; in fewer than three exchanges, Wei Yan cut him down from his horse with a single stroke. The deputy vanguard commander Zhu Zan led his troops onward in pursuit, when suddenly another body of soldiers swept into view; the great general at their head was Zhao Yun. Zhu Zan was caught unprepared and Zhao Yun thrust him dead with a single spear stroke. Seeing that both vanguard forces had been defeated, Cao Zhen and Guo Huai sought to recall their troops and withdraw; but behind them arose deafening battle cries and a clamor of drums and horns. Guan Xing’s and Zhang Bao’s forces charged out from two directions, surrounded Cao Zhen and Guo Huai, and dealt their men a savage beating. Cao and Guo led their defeated troops in breaking through the encirclement and escaped. The Shu forces won a complete victory, pursued the enemy all the way to the Wei River, and seized the Wei camp. Cao Zhen grieved without end over the loss of his two vanguard commanders; he had no choice but to submit a memorial to the court requesting reinforcements.

p.src: Meanwhile, the ruler of Wei, Cao Rui, was holding court when a close attendant memorialized: “The Commander-in-Chief Cao Zhen has suffered repeated defeats at the hands of Shu and lost two vanguard commanders, while countless Qiang soldiers have also perished. The situation is most urgent. He has now submitted a memorial seeking aid. We ask Your Majesty to decide what is to be done.” Cao Rui was greatly alarmed and urgently asked for a plan to repel the enemy. Hua Xin memorialized: “Your Majesty must personally lead a campaign and summon all the lords to a great muster. Only when every man gives his utmost can the enemy be repelled. Otherwise, Chang’an will be lost, and the region within the passes will be imperiled.” The Grand Tutor Zhong Yao memorialized: “A commander who knows more than others can master them. Master Sun says, ‘Know the enemy and know yourself, and you will triumph in a hundred battles.’ In my judgment, though Cao Zhen has long experience in war, he is no match for Zhuge Liang. At the risk of every member of my household, high and low, I recommend one man who can repel the Shu army. I do not know whether it will please Your Majesty to approve.” Cao Rui said, “You are a venerable elder and a founding minister. What worthy man can repel the Shu army? Summon him quickly to share Our burden.” Zhong Yao memorialized: “Previously, when Zhuge Liang wished to raise an army and invade our borders, he feared this man alone. He therefore spread false rumors, causing Your Majesty to suspect and dismiss him; only then did he dare advance deep into our territory. If he is now restored to service, Zhuge Liang will withdraw of his own accord.” Cao Rui asked who the man was. Zhong Yao replied, “It is Sima Yi, General-in-Chief of Agile Cavalry.” Cao Rui sighed and said, “I, too, regret that affair. Where is Zhongda now?” Zhong Yao replied, “I recently heard that Zhongda is living in retirement at Wancheng.” Cao Rui immediately issued an edict and sent an envoy bearing the imperial tally to restore Sima Yi to office and appoint him Pacification Commander of the West, with orders to mobilize all the forces around Nanyang and proceed to Chang’an. Cao Rui would personally lead the campaign and ordered Sima Yi to arrive there by the appointed day for the muster. The imperial envoy hastened day and night to Wancheng.

p.src: Meanwhile, since taking the field, Kongming had won a succession of complete victories and was greatly pleased; while he was gathered with his officers in the camp at Mount Qi to discuss military affairs, a sudden report announced that Li Feng, son of Li Yan, the commander guarding the Yong’an Palace, had come to see him. Kongming supposed that Eastern Wu had invaded the border. Deeply alarmed and suspicious, he summoned Li Feng into the tent and questioned him. Li Feng said, “I have come especially to bring glad tidings.” Kongming asked, “What glad tidings?” Li Feng replied, “When Meng Da surrendered to Wei in former days, he did so only because he had no choice. At that time Cao Pi admired his ability, frequently bestowed fine horses, gold, and pearls upon him, and even rode with him in the same imperial carriage. He appointed him Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and Administrator of Xincheng, placing him in command of Shangyong, Jincheng, and other districts and entrusting him with responsibility for the southwest. Since Cao Pi’s death and Cao Rui’s accession, however, many at court have grown jealous of him. Meng Da has known no peace by day or night and often tells his officers, ‘I was originally a general of Shu; circumstances forced me into my present position.’ He has now repeatedly sent trusted men with letters to my father, asking him to inform the Prime Minister at the earliest opportunity that he already entertained this intention when the five armies invaded the River Lands; now, at Xincheng, having learned that the Prime Minister is campaigning against Wei, he wishes to raise the forces of Jincheng, Xincheng, and Shangyong, launch an uprising there, and march directly upon Luoyang; while the Prime Minister takes Chang’an, thus securing both capitals. I have now brought the messenger and all the letters he sent on successive occasions for your inspection.” Kongming was overjoyed and richly rewarded Li Feng and the others. Suddenly, a spy entered and reported: “The ruler of Wei, Cao Rui, is proceeding in person to Chang’an; at the same time, he has issued an edict restoring Sima Yi to office and appointing him Pacification Commander of the West, with orders to raise the local troops and muster at Chang’an.” Kongming was greatly alarmed. The staff officer Ma Su said, “Cao Rui is hardly worth speaking of! If he comes to Chang’an, we can capture him there. Why should the Prime Minister be alarmed?” Kongming replied, “Do you think I fear Cao Rui? The only man who troubles me is Sima Yi. Meng Da now intends to undertake a great enterprise, but if he encounters Sima Yi, his plan is certain to fail. Meng Da is no match for Sima Yi and will surely be captured by him. If Meng Da dies, the Central Plains will not be easily won.” Ma Su said, “Why not write an urgent letter instructing Meng Da to take precautions?” Kongming followed his advice and immediately wrote a letter, ordering the messenger to hurry back through the night and report to Meng Da.

p.src: When Kongming had finished reading, he flung the letter to the ground, stamped his foot, and cried, “Meng Da will surely die at Sima Yi's hand!” Ma Su asked, “Why do you say so, Prime Minister?” Kongming replied, “The Art of War says, ‘Attack where the enemy is unprepared; appear where you are unexpected.’ How could the timing possibly be fixed at one month? Since Cao Rui has entrusted Sima Yi with command and empowered him to destroy any foe he encounters, why would Sima Yi wait to submit a memorial? If he learns that Meng Da has rebelled, his army will certainly arrive within ten days. How could Meng Da possibly make ready in time?” All the commanders acknowledged the force of his reasoning. Kongming urgently instructed the messenger to report back: “If the rising has not yet begun, you must on no account let your fellow conspirators know of it. If they learn of it, you will certainly fail.” The man bowed farewell and returned to Xincheng.

p.src: Meanwhile, Sima Yi was living at leisure in Wancheng. Hearing that the armies of Wei had repeatedly been defeated by Shu, he raised his face to heaven and sighed deeply. Sima Yi's eldest son was Sima Shi, styled Ziyuan; his second son was Sima Zhao, styled Zishang. Both had long harbored great ambitions and were well versed in military writings. That day they were attending at his side. Seeing him sigh, they asked, “Father, why do you sigh?” Sima Yi said, “What would you boys know of great affairs?” Sima Shi said, “Can it be that you lament the ruler of Wei's refusal to employ you?” Sima Zhao laughed and said, “Sooner or later, a summons for Father is certain to come.” Before he had finished speaking, it was suddenly reported that an imperial envoy had arrived bearing the tally of authority. After hearing the edict, Sima Yi began mobilizing all the forces around Wancheng. Then another report came: a member of the household of Shen Yi, Administrator of Jincheng, sought an audience on a confidential matter. Sima Yi had the man brought into a private chamber and questioned him. The man gave a detailed account of Meng Da's intended rebellion. He also produced a written denunciation supported by Li Fu, Meng Da's trusted subordinate, and Deng Xian, Meng Da's nephew. When Sima Yi had heard everything, he raised a hand to his brow and exclaimed, “This is truly our sovereign's boundless, heaven-high good fortune! Zhuge Liang's army is at Qishan and has struck terror into everyone within and beyond the court; His Majesty has now been forced to proceed to Chang'an. Had he failed to employ me at this critical hour, one stroke from Meng Da would have brought down both capitals! That traitor must be conspiring with Zhuge Liang. If I seize him first, Zhuge Liang will certainly lose heart and withdraw of his own accord.” His eldest son, Sima Shi, said, “Father, you should quickly write a memorial and report this to the Son of Heaven.” Sima Yi replied, “If we wait for the imperial command, a month will pass in going and returning, and it will be too late.” He immediately ordered the troops to set out and cover two days' march each day, decreeing death for any delay; at the same time, he sent Staff Officer Liang Ji racing through the night to Xincheng with a dispatch ordering Meng Da and the others to prepare for the campaign, so that Meng Da would suspect nothing.

p.src: Liang Ji went on ahead, and Sima Yi followed with the army. After two days' march, an army emerged from below a hillside. It was led by General of the Right Xu Huang, who dismounted to greet Sima Yi and said, “His Majesty has reached Chang'an and is personally resisting the Shu army. Where are you going now, Commander?” Sima Yi said quietly, “Meng Da has rebelled, and I am going to seize him.” Xu Huang said, “I volunteer to lead the vanguard.” Sima Yi was delighted and joined their forces together. Xu Huang commanded the van, Sima Yi the center, while Sima Yi's two sons guarded the rear. After another two days, the vanguard scouts captured Meng Da's trusted messenger, found Kongming's reply upon him, and brought him before Sima Yi. Sima Yi said, “I will not kill you. Tell me everything from the beginning.” The man had no choice but to relate, one by one, all that had passed between Kongming and Meng Da. After reading Kongming's reply, Sima Yi exclaimed in astonishment, “All capable men under heaven see things alike. Kongming discerned my plan before I could act. Fortunately, through the Son of Heaven's good fortune, we have obtained this intelligence. Meng Da can do nothing now.” He then urged the army onward through the night.

p.src: Meanwhile, in Xincheng, Meng Da had arranged with Shen Yi, Administrator of Jincheng, and Shen Dan, Administrator of Shangyong, to rise on an appointed day. Shen Dan and Shen Yi pretended to consent and drilled their troops each day, waiting only for the Wei army to arrive so they could respond from within; but they reported to Meng Da that their weapons and provisions were not yet fully prepared and that they dared not fix a date for the rising. Meng Da believed them without suspicion. Suddenly it was reported that Staff Officer Liang Ji had arrived, and Meng Da welcomed him into the city. Liang Ji conveyed Sima Yi's order: “Commander Sima has received an imperial edict and is now mobilizing troops from every quarter to repel the Shu army. You, Administrator, are to assemble the troops under your command and await deployment.” Meng Da asked, “On what day did the Commander set out?” Liang Ji replied, “By now he has probably left Wancheng and gone toward Chang'an.” Meng Da rejoiced inwardly, saying, “My great undertaking is as good as accomplished!” He gave a banquet for Liang Ji and escorted him beyond the walls. Then he notified Shen Yi and Shen Dan that they would rise the next day, raise the banners of the Great Han, send out all their troops, and march directly on Luoyang. Suddenly it was reported that dust was billowing skyward beyond the walls, though no one knew whence the troops had come. Meng Da climbed the wall to look and saw a powerful force racing toward the city beneath banners inscribed “General of the Right Xu Huang.” Meng Da was greatly alarmed and hastily raised the drawbridge. Xu Huang could not rein in his mount and came straight to the edge of the moat, where he shouted, “Meng Da, rebel and traitor! Surrender at once!” Enraged, Meng Da hastily drew his bow and shot, striking Xu Huang squarely in the forehead. The Wei commanders rescued him and carried him away. A storm of arrows descended from the walls, and only then did the Wei troops withdraw. Just as Meng Da was about to open the gates and give chase, banners covered the sky on every side: Sima Yi's army had arrived. Meng Da raised his face to heaven and sighed, “It has happened exactly as Kongming foretold!” He therefore shut the gates and held the city fast.

Shen Dan and Shen Yi shouted, “Rebel, do not flee! Come quickly and receive your death!” Seeing that circumstances had changed, Meng Da wheeled his horse and fled toward the city, but a storm of arrows descended from the walls. Li Fu and Deng Xian threw open the city gates and welcomed Sima Yi into the city. After reassuring the people and rewarding the troops, Sima Yi sent a messenger to report the outcome to Cao Rui, ruler of Wei.
